item.title: Anchorage Digital Sets Up Asset Manager to Offer Bitcoin Yield to Clients
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Anchorage Digital Sets Up Asset Manager to Offer Bitcoin Yield to Clients Anchorage Digital, the first federally chartered crypto bank in the U.S., is moving into asset management with a new subsidiary that will offer custody clients a way to earn yield on their bitcoin. The unit, called 61st Parallel Asset Management, is expected to start operating by early December, CEO Nathan McCauley said in an interview to CoinDesk. Its first product will be a bitcoin-denominated fund, meaning returns are measured in BTC rather than dollars. The name nods to the city of Anchorage, Alaska, which sits at 61 degrees north latitude. “We have increasingly heard clients say they want to earn on top of the assets they hold at Anchorage — something that’s very common among the large financial institutions of the world,” McCauley said. Anchorage has filed a Form ADV, the disclosure document investment advisers use to register with the Securities and Exchange Commission or state regulators, or to report as exempt advisers. The form covers a firm’s ownership, business, assets under management, fees and conflicts of interest. As of Tuesday afternoon, the SEC’s public adviser database showed no record for 61st Parallel, so the filing’s details were not yet public. Paperwork dating back to summer The entity itself is not new. New York state records show that 61st Parallel Asset Management LLC, a Delaware company, registered to do business in New York on July 8, listing an office on Park Avenue South in Manhattan. Anchorage already lets clients earn on some holdings. Its website lists staking, which pays rewards for helping secure proof-of-stake networks, and a separate rewards product for eligible assets. Bitcoin runs on proof-of-work and cannot be staked natively. Anchorage has not said publicly how the fund will generate yield, what it will charge or which clients will qualify. Those details matter to bitcoin holders, because bitcoin pays no interest on its own. Common ways to earn on it include lending coins out, posting them as collateral or selling options against them, and each carries its own risk. Public companies have already tested some of those approaches. Trump Media disclosed this month that it had pledged about 73% of its bitcoin to an options program in which the counterparty can rehypothecate, or reuse, the coins. From custodian to full-service bank Founded in 2017, Anchorage received a national trust bank charter from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency in January 2021, the first crypto firm to win one. The OCC lifted a 2022 consent order over the bank’s anti-money laundering controls in August 2025. The bank no longer stands alone. Last December, the OCC granted conditional approvals to five more digital asset firms, including Circle, Ripple, BitGo, Paxos and Fidelity Digital Assets, to become national trust banks. item.title: Coldcard Postmortem Says Weak Seeds, Not Hacked Devices, Drove Bitcoin Thefts
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Coldcard Postmortem Says Weak Seeds, Not Hacked Devices, Drove Bitcoin Thefts Coinkite on Tuesday published its full postmortem on the Coldcard seed-generation flaw that let thieves drain bitcoin from customer wallets starting in July, saying no device was hacked and that the stolen keys were rebuilt offline from weak seeds. The 18-page report , dated Nov. 23 and modeled on a National Transportation Safety Board accident report, lays out how the defect shipped in Coldcard firmware from March 29, 2021, through July 30, 2026, and why years of outside reviews missed it. “The losses are real and, for some customers, life-changing. No report or firmware update can undo that. We are sorry,” Coinkite wrote. A silent swap in the random number generator A seed is the list of recovery words that controls a bitcoin wallet, and it is only as safe as the randomness used to create it. Coldcard devices were supposed to draw that randomness from the hardware random number generator built into their STM32 chip. Instead, a firmware setting switched that hardware source off, and a safeguard in Coinkite’s libNgU code library failed to catch it. Seed generation quietly fell back to Yasmarang, a predictable software generator built into MicroPython, the programming environment the firmware runs on. Nothing crashed, and the devices produced normal-looking seed words. Coinkite estimates affected seeds carried roughly 40 bits of effective security on the older Mk2 and Mk3 models and about 72 bits on the Mk4, Mk5 and Q, against an intended 128 bits. That shrinks the pool of possible seeds enough for attackers to search it offline. The report says Coinkite’s release checks confirmed the hardware code was present, but never confirmed that seed generation actually reached it. At least 15 independent review efforts since 2021 also missed the flaw, including two paid third-party reviews and an AI-assisted firmware review this year that produced 85 candidate findings. Hundreds of Coldcard owners report losses Unexpected transactions from affected seeds began July 29. Coinkite said it identified the defect the next day, after users discovered thefts, and shipped fixed firmware for every supported release track on July 31. As of Nov. 18, Coinkite had received about 300 loss-related support tickets tied to 242 customer accounts, or about 0.21% of its estimated Coldcard user base. The company’s blog post cites 236 accounts. Because Coldcard is self-custodial, Coinkite can only count losses that customers report, and it says the true number is likely higher. The report cites Galaxy Research figures showing 1,778.84 BTC stolen from more than 8,600 addresses, worth about $107 million at today’s price. Galaxy pegged losses above $115 million in August, based on prices when the coins were taken, and white hats later moved some exposed coins into a recovery trust. item.title: Stacks Opens Bond 4 With 1,050 BTC of Bitcoin Staking Capacity
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Stacks Opens Bond 4 With 1,050 BTC of Bitcoin Staking Capacity GRAND CAYMAN, Cayman Islands, Nov. 24, 2026. Stacks Labs today announced 1,050 BTC of capacity for Bond 4 of Bitcoin staking with Stacks, a Bitcoin layer where BTC holders earn BTC. The bond starts ~Dec. 5, and institutions can register at stacks.co/institutional-bitcoin-staking. Bond 4 carries a 3% target annual yield, paid in BTC weekly over a six-month term. Each BTC staked is paired with STX worth 5% of its value, so filling Bond 4’s 1,050 BTC of capacity requires a corresponding STX commitment. Rewards come from Stacks miners, who commit BTC through Proof of Transfer (PoX), the consensus mechanism Stacks has run since January 2021. Every bond since the Genesis Bond launched in September has filled. 21shares returned for Bond 3, and Bullish (NYSE: BLSH) joined as the first top-10 public Bitcoin treasury company to stake BTC. “Opening more than 1,000 BTC of new capacity for institutions shows how strong the demand for Bitcoin yield has become,” said Muneeb Ali, CEO, Stacks Labs, and founder of Stacks. Institutions can stake from qualified custody, including BitGo. During the bootstrap phase, self-custodial Bitcoin staking is whitelisted. Holders who are not on the whitelist can take part through pooled Bitcoin staking at stacks.co/bitcoin-staking . About Stacks Stacks is a Bitcoin layer where BTC holders earn BTC. With Bitcoin staking, holders stake BTC with STX, and their BTC stays on the Bitcoin L1 under their own custody. Stacks has distributed over 4,200 BTC in rewards to participants since 2021. item.title: UniCredit Opens Bitcoin to Italian Savers, Capping Gains at 65%
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine UniCredit Opens Bitcoin to Italian Savers, Capping Gains at 65% UniCredit on Tuesday began selling a capital-protected certificate that lets retail clients in Italy follow the bitcoin price, a product the bank calls the first investment solution of its kind in the country. The six-year, euro-denominated certificate will be listed on the Munich stock exchange and is linked to the iShares Bitcoin ETP managed by BlackRock, UniCredit said in a release. The placement period runs from Nov. 24 to Dec. 18, 2026. The note is open only to UniCredit Italia retail clients with specific characteristics, and only through the bank’s advisory service. It can’t be bought independently or by investors who aren’t UniCredit clients, and the minimum investment is €1,000, Italian newswire Teleborsa reported . How the certificate works A capital-protected certificate is a structured note. The issuing bank promises to repay the original investment at maturity and pays a return tied to an underlying asset, in this case bitcoin through the BlackRock product. Buyers hold a claim on the bank, not bitcoin itself. If bitcoin is down at maturity, holders get 100% of their capital back. If it rises, they share in the gain up to a maximum return of 65% on the capital invested. Before maturity, the certificate’s price follows market conditions, so the protection applies only at the end of the six years. That cap works out to roughly 8.7% a year at most, no matter how far bitcoin climbs. And because the certificate is UniCredit’s own debt, the protection depends on the bank’s ability to pay. Documents for a similar UniCredit note in Germany state that no third-party guarantee covers an issuer default. “With the launch of this certificate, UniCredit is writing a new page of financial innovation in the country, confirming its market leadership,” said Chicco Di Stasi, Head of Group Investment Product Solutions at UniCredit. “Diversification is no longer just a prudential rule, but the key to capturing the value of the future,” Di Stasi said, adding that the bank is responding to growing client demand and offering the product to Italian savers “for the very first time.” Built on notes sold in Germany and Austria Di Stasi said the bank is bringing to Italy “a pioneering model already proven by its success in Germany and Austria.” Those earlier notes are denominated in dollars and track BlackRock’s U.S.-listed iShares Bitcoin Trust instead. HypoVereinsbank, UniCredit’s German unit, sold a version to private clients in March with a 160% cap, or 60% upside. UniCredit Bank Austria launched its own six-year note in April with a 175% cap, or 75% upside. Italy’s 65% falls between the two. The bank has moved into bitcoin in steps. It first offered a capital-protected bitcoin product to professional clients only in 2025. In May, it placed a bitcoin and ether certificate for professional clients with a €100,000 minimum.
